name: Hunnic Empire (Attila)
summary: Nomadic Huns crossed the Volga around 370, subdued the Alans and Goths and by the 420s were based on the Great Hungarian Plain, extorting tribute from both halves of the Roman Empire. Under Attila (sole ruler from c. 445) they ravaged the Balkans, Gaul and Italy, but after his death in 453 the subject peoples revolted at the Nedao and the empire fell apart; his son Dengizich was killed in 469.

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the West and under Justinian I reconquered North Africa, Italy and southern Spain, reaching its greatest extent in 565. The Arab conquests of the 630s–640s stripped away Syria and Egypt; the Macedonian emperors recovered ground up to Basil II's conquest of Bulgaria, before Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to the Turks. Sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 and restored from Nicaea in 1261, the shrunken state fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

name: Tang China
summary: Founded in 618 by Li Yuan amid the collapse of the Sui (the map starts in 623), the Tang destroyed the Eastern Turks, conquered the Tarim Basin and, with Silla, Goguryeo, pushing protectorates as far as Central Asia. Defeat at Talas (751) and the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) ended this expansion, after which Tibet and regional governors ate into Tang power. The Huang Chao rebellion devastated the empire and the last emperor was deposed in 907.

name: Tibetan Empire
summary: Under Songtsen Gampo (r. c. 618–650) the Yarlung kings united the Tibetan Plateau, moved their seat to Lhasa and absorbed Zhangzhung and the Tuyuhun. Tibet contested the Tarim Basin with Tang China for two centuries, briefly occupied Chang'an in 763 and reached its greatest extent in the early 800s. After the murder of Ralpachen (838) and the assassination of Langdarma in 842 the empire broke apart.

name: Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates
summary: After Muhammad's death in 632 the first caliphs, ruling from Medina, united Arabia and within twenty years took Syria and Egypt from Byzantium and destroyed the Sasanian Empire. From 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus and pushed the conquests to Spain, Sindh and Central Asia, creating one of the largest empires yet seen (c. 11 million km² by 720). Defeats at Constantinople (718) and Tours (732), the Berber revolt and civil wars sapped the dynasty, and the Abbasids overthrew it in 750.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, founded Baghdad in 762 and under al-Mansur, Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun presided over a vast empire and a golden age of learning. From the 9th century provinces broke away (Aghlabids, Tahirids, Tulunids, then the Fatimids), and after 945 the caliphs were figureheads under the Buyids and then the Seljuks; the map shows no Abbasid territory between 970 and 1201. Caliph al-Nasir revived a small state in Iraq, but the Mongols sacked Baghdad and killed the last caliph in 1258.

name: Carolingian Empire (Charlemagne)
summary: Pepin the Short replaced the Merovingians as king of the Franks in 751, and his son Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom, Saxony and the Avar lands, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. After the civil war that followed Louis the Pious's death, the Treaty of Verdun (843) split the empire among his three sons. Charles the Fat reunited it in 884, but he was deposed in 887 and the empire dissolved for good on his death in 888.

name: Ghana Empire (Wagadu)
summary: The Soninke kingdom of Ghana, between the Senegal and Niger rivers, grew rich on the trans-Saharan gold trade and was already known to Arab writers as the 'Land of Gold' in the 8th century. It peaked in the 10th–11th centuries, seized the trading town of Awdaghust in 990 and was described in detail by al-Bakri in 1068. Its rulers converted to Islam around 1076 (whether the Almoravids conquered it is disputed); weakened, it was overrun by the Sosso by 1203 and later absorbed into Mali.

name: Khmer Empire
summary: Jayavarman II's consecration as universal monarch on Phnom Kulen in 802 founded the Angkorian empire, and Yasovarman I built the first capital at Angkor. Suryavarman II (builder of Angkor Wat) and Jayavarman VII (Angkor Thom, the Bayon) led its high point, including the conquest of Champa after the Cham sack of Angkor in 1177. From the 14th century the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya pressed in, and Angkor was abandoned after its fall in 1431.

name: Chola Empire
summary: Vijayalaya re-founded Chola power at Thanjavur around 848, and his successors overcame the Pandyas and Pallavas. Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044) made it the leading power of South India and the Bay of Bengal, taking Sri Lanka and the Maldives, marching to the Ganges and raiding Srivijaya in 1025. The Later Cholas held most of the Tamil country after 1070, but Pandya attacks from 1215–16 broke the empire; the map ends in 1259, and the last king, Rajendra III, is last recorded in 1279.

name: Holy Roman Empire
summary: Otto I's imperial coronation in 962 joined the German kingdom to Italy, and Burgundy was added in 1032, making the empire the strongest monarchy in western Europe into the 13th century. Clashes with the papacy and the collapse of Hohenstaufen power after 1250 left the princes increasingly independent, a system fixed by the Golden Bull of 1356 and the reforms of 1495. The Reformation and the Thirty Years' War further weakened imperial authority; Westphalia (1648) recognised the loss of Switzerland and the Dutch Netherlands, and Francis II dissolved the empire in 1806.

name: Great Seljuk Empire
summary: Oghuz Turks led by Tughril and Chaghri took Merv and Nishapur in 1037–38, crushed the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan and in 1055 entered Baghdad as protectors of the Abbasid caliph. Alp Arslan's victory at Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia, and under Malik-Shah and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk the empire stretched from the Levant to Central Asia. After 1092 it fragmented among rival heirs; Sanjar's defeat at Qatwan (1141) and capture by the Oghuz (1153) ended Seljuk power in the east, and the last sultan fell to the Khwarazmians in 1194, leaving only the Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia (to 1308).

name: Mongol Empire
summary: Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin united the steppe and conquered northern China and the Khwarazmian Empire; his successors took the Jin, Rus' and the Abbasid caliphate, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history. After Möngke's death in 1259 the Toluid civil war split the empire into the Yuan dynasty and three western khanates (the Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate and Ilkhanate). Kublai completed the conquest of Song China in 1279, but his attacks on Japan failed, and by his death in 1294 the four khanates went their own way.

name: Delhi Sultanate
summary: Founded in 1206 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak in the Indian lands of the Ghurids, the sultanate was ruled in turn by the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties. Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq pushed its armies deep into the south, briefly ruling most of the subcontinent, but rebellions created the Bahmani, Vijayanagara and other independent states. Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left a small kingdom that the Lodis partly revived, until Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

name: Mali Empire
summary: Sundiata Keita's victory over the Sosso at Kirina (c. 1235) founded the Mali Empire, which absorbed old Ghana and controlled the gold and salt trade of the western Sahel. It peaked in the 14th century under Mansa Musa, whose 1324 pilgrimage through Cairo became legendary, and Sulayman, whose court Ibn Battuta visited. After 1360 weak rulers, Tuareg and Mossi raids and the rise of Songhai cost it Timbuktu, Gao and the north; a last attempt to take Djenné failed in 1599 and the empire broke up after Mahmud IV's death c. 1610.

name: Aztec Empire
summary: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325, and served the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco until they overthrew them in 1428 and formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan. Under Itzcoatl, Moctezuma I, Axayacatl and Ahuitzotl the alliance built a tributary empire across central Mexico to the Gulf, Oaxaca and Soconusco, though it was halted by the Purépecha in the west. Cortés arrived in 1519 with Indigenous allies; after smallpox and a long siege, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, after the map ends.

name: Timurid Empire
summary: Timur took control of the western Chagatai lands around 1370 (the map starts in 1375) and in three decades of campaigns conquered Iran and Iraq, broke the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi, Damascus and Baghdad and defeated the Ottomans at Ankara. After his death in 1405 his son Shah Rukh ruled from Herat over a smaller realm that saw the Timurid Renaissance. Civil wars, the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu cost the dynasty western Iran, and the Uzbeks took Samarkand (1501) and Herat (1507); Babur, a Timurid, went on to found the Mughal Empire.

name: Inca Empire
summary: After defeating the Chanka, Pachacuti (traditionally from 1438) turned the kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, and he and his son Topa Inca conquered the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile, including the coastal kingdom of Chimor. At its height under Huayna Capac it was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Disease and a succession war between Huáscar and Atahualpa weakened it just as Pizarro arrived; Atahualpa was seized at Cajamarca in 1532 and executed in 1533, though Inca resistance continued at Vilcabamba until 1572.

name: Songhai Empire
summary: From Gao, Sonni Ali (r. 1464–1492) turned Songhai into the Sahel's leading power, taking Timbuktu and Djenné and much of Mali's former territory. Askia Muhammad I, who seized power in 1493, reorganised the state, made a celebrated pilgrimage to Mecca and pushed its frontiers further. After his overthrow in 1528 civil wars weakened the empire, and in 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms routed the Songhai at Tondibi and sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.
